bites.title: Exceptions and error messages
bites.body:
An exception is Python's way of saying "I cannot continue with this". The program stops what it was doing and reports what went wrong, like a smoke alarm: unpleasant, but far better than a silent fire.

The message has a type and a detail. KeyError: 'name' means you asked a dictionary for a label it does not have. TypeError means the wrong kind of value was used. FileNotFoundError means what it says.

Code can catch exceptions with try and except to respond sensibly: try the risky step, and if it fails in an expected way, do something else.

Read error messages properly. They are usually the fastest route to the fix.
bites.sourceNote: Python tutorial, errors and exceptions · confidence: high

choices.text: The file called name is missing
The code asked a dictionary for the key 'name' and it was not there
The program ran out of memory

questions.explanation: A KeyError names the dictionary key that was requested but does not exist.

bites.title: Retries and timeouts
bites.body: A timeout stops a call that might wait forever. A retry tries again after a failure, usually with a pause that grows — backoff — so you do not hammer a sick server. Retrying a read is usually safe. Retrying a payment or a "create" can do the action twice if the first one actually succeeded. That idea is called idempotency: doing it twice should not matter, or you should not blindly retry.
bites.sourceNote: Conceptual notes on timeouts, backoff, and idempotency · confidence: high

choices.text: To make a successful call run twice
To stop waiting after a set time

questions.explanation: A timeout bounds the wait. Without one, a stuck call can stall the program.

questions.prompt: Why be careful retrying a request that creates something?

choices.text: The first try may have succeeded, so a retry can create a second one

questions.explanation: If the response was lost but the server did the work, a blind retry repeats a side effect.

bites.title: Retries and timeouts (concept)
bites.body:
Networks fail in small, temporary ways all the time. Two tools deal with that.

A timeout is a limit on waiting: "if there is no answer in 30 seconds, give up". Without one, a program can hang forever, like staying on hold with no intention of ever putting the phone down.

A retry is trying again after a failure. Good retries wait a little longer each time (1 second, 2, 4), which is called exponential backoff. That gives a struggling service room to recover instead of piling on.

And retries need a cap. Three to five attempts is typical. After that, stop and report the failure.
bites.sourceNote: Drafted by AI, November 2026 · confidence: high

choices.text: Retrying instantly as fast as possible
Waiting longer between each retry, for example 1, 2, then 4 seconds
Halving the timeout on every attempt

questions.explanation: Backoff increases the pause between attempts so a struggling service is not flooded with retries.

bites.title: Retry timeouts and rate limits; do not retry bad input
bites.body:
Not every failure deserves a second try. The question is: would the same request succeed if I simply sent it again later?

Yes, for temporary problems: a timeout, a 429 rate limit, a 500 server error. The request was fine and the moment was bad.

No, for a bad request: a 400 for malformed input, a 401 for a wrong key, a 404 for a wrong address. Sending it again will fail the same way, however many times you try.

It is like a locked shop door. If the shop is closed for lunch, come back later. If you have the wrong address, coming back later will not help.
bites.sourceNote: Drafted by AI, November 2026 · confidence: high

questions.prompt: Which error is worth retrying after a short wait?
questions.explanation: A 429 is temporary and clears with time. The others mean the request itself is wrong and will keep failing.

bites.title: Log errors with enough context to find the cause
bites.body:
A log is a written record of what a program did. When something fails at 3 a.m. and nobody is watching, the log is the only witness.

A useless entry says "Error occurred". A useful one says what was being attempted, with which input, when, and the full error: "Failed to summarise document 4812 for user 77: timeout after 30s".

Think of a doctor's notes. "Patient unwell" helps nobody. Symptoms, time and what was tried lets the next person carry on.

One firm limit: never log secrets or private data. API keys, passwords and personal details do not belong in log files.
bites.sourceNote: Drafted by AI, November 2026 · confidence: high

questions.prompt: Which log entry is most useful for finding a problem later?
questions.explanation: A good entry says what was being done, to which item, and exactly how it failed.

bites.title: Failing clearly beats failing silently
bites.body:
The worst bug is not the crash. It is the code that hits a problem, hides it, and carries on with wrong data.

The usual culprit in generated code looks like this: try: ... except: pass. It means "if anything at all goes wrong, say nothing". The program looks healthy while quietly producing rubbish.

Compare a car with a broken fuel gauge that always shows half full. You would much rather have the warning light.

A clear failure stops and says what went wrong and where. That is something you can fix. So when you review AI-written code, treat an empty except block as a red flag and ask what should really happen there.
bites.sourceNote: Drafted by AI, November 2026 · confidence: high

choices.text: It hides every error, so the program continues with missing or wrong data
It makes the program run slowly

questions.explanation: Swallowing all exceptions removes the signal that something failed, so bad results spread unnoticed.
